questions.question: What assumptions produced the modeled 1.15-copy, 95%-probability LOD for the first primer pool?

options.A: 172 primer pairs averaging 99 bp, 6% single-strand cDNA amplification efficiency, and 80% target success
options.B: 171 primer pairs averaging 158 bp, 26% efficiency, and 100% target success
options.C: 28 targets at 99% efficiency and no failed amplicons
options.D: One RT-PCR amplicon at 6% efficiency with 50% genome recovery

questions.rationale: The model combines the 172-pair panel design with conservative amplification and target-recovery assumptions.
questions.evidence_quote: We designed a panel of 172 pairs of multiplex PCR primers in order to increase the sensitivity of detecting SARS-CoV-2 (Fig. 1B ). The average amplicon length is 99bp. The amplicons span across the entire SARS-CoV-2 genome with an average 76bp gap (76±10bp) between adjacent amplicons. Since the observed efficiency of multiplex PCR is about 26% in amplifying the four DNA strands of a pair of human chromosomes, we assumed an efficiency of 6% in amplifying the single-strand of a cDNA molecule. In addition, it has already been reported that 79% of variants are recovered when directly amplifying 600 amplicons from a single cell using our technology 37 . Therefore, we assumed that 80% of targeted regions would be amplified successfully. Using the same mathematical model described above, we estimated that our SARS-CoV-2 panel can detect 1.15 copies of the virus at 95% probability

questions.question: Why did a second overlapping primer pool improve the modeled detection limit beyond the first pool?

options.A: Its 171 pairs targeted gaps in the 172-pair pool, together providing full-genome coverage and a modeled 0.29-copy LOD
options.B: It doubled the length of every first-pool amplicon and raised efficiency to 99%
options.C: It amplified only the S gene, eliminating the N-gene targets
options.D: It increased the first pool from 172 to 343 pairs without overlap

questions.rationale: The second pool was deliberately complementary to first-pool gaps, increasing the chance of at least one target occurrence.
questions.evidence_quote: We also designed a second pool of 171 multiplex PCR primer pairs. The target regions of these primer pairs overlap with the gaps between target regions of the previous pool of 172 primer pairs (Fig. 1B ). Together, these two overlapping pools of primers provide full coverage of the entire viral genome. Most importantly, using both pools in detection would lead to a calculated detection limit of 0.29 copies at 95% probability.

questions.question: What role did electrophoresis play relative to sequencing in the diagnostic workflow?

options.A: Defined-size peaks gave a fast indication of a coronavirus-family positive, while NGS identified the specific virus
options.B: Electrophoresis alone identified SARS-CoV-2 uniquely, making NGS unnecessary
options.C: NGS was used only to size amplicons, while electrophoresis detected mutations
options.D: Neither was used until after clinical sequencing was complete

questions.rationale: The authors distinguish rapid amplicon-pattern screening from definitive virus identification by sequencing.
questions.evidence_quote: Since dozens of target regions could be amplified from a single copy of SARS-CoV-2, electrophoresis peaks with a defined distribution of peak sizes were expected. Multiplex PCR could potentially amplify not only SARS-CoV-2, but also other coronaviruses, due to shared sequence similarities despite the fact that we designed primers specific to the SARS-CoV-2 genome to avoid cross amplification. In that context, electrophoresis analysis provides a fast and sensitive indication of infection from at least that family of viruses. For specificity, the generated NGS sequencing library can be interrogated for definitive identification of the specific virus.

questions.question: How did the single-copy plasmid experiment compare the modeled and observed probability of detecting about 1.1 copies?

options.A: The model predicted 12% detection after sampling probability, but the experiment observed 56%
options.B: The model predicted 56%, but the experiment observed 12%
options.C: Both model and experiment predicted exactly 100% detection
options.D: The model predicted 26% and no experiment was conducted

questions.rationale: The observed detection rate was substantially higher than predicted, indicating the assumed 6% single-strand efficiency was conservative.
questions.evidence_quote: The theoretical calculation gives a 66% probability to sample 1.1 copies, and a 12% chance to detect them based on a multiplex PCR efficiency of 6%. In practice, we experimentally observed a significantly higher 56% probability to detect 1.1 copies (Fig. 2C ). These results suggest that the efficiency of multiplex PCR is actually higher than the previously estimated 6% when a single-stranded cDNA molecule is amplified.

questions.question: At what plasmid input did library recovery become incomplete, and how steep was the drop?

options.A: About 96% of amplicons at 14 copies, 77% at 2.8 copies, and 37% at 0.6 copies
options.B: About 37% at 14 copies, 77% at 2.8 copies, and 96% at 0.6 copies
options.C: All amplicons were recovered at 0.6 copies and none at 14 copies
options.D: About 96% were recovered at 1,700 copies, but no lower-input tests were performed

questions.rationale: The amplicon recovery fraction decreases sharply at low copy number, despite high sensitivity for detecting a positive signal.
questions.evidence_quote: Approximately 96% of the amplicons were recovered with 14 copies of plasmids, 77% with 2.8 copies, and 37% with 0.6 copies (Fig. 2E ).

questions.question: What coverage did the two-pool assay achieve for the lowest-load clinical specimen?

options.A: About 95% of the genome at 100X for 8 copies, versus 98–99% for 22–675,885 copies
options.B: Only 58% at 100X for 8 copies, regardless of higher loads
options.C: 100% at 100X for 8 copies and 95% for all higher loads
options.D: About 95% at 5,000X for 8 copies, with no coverage at higher loads

questions.rationale: The 13-specimen sequencing study reports high coverage at 100-fold depth even at the lowest measured viral load.
questions.evidence_quote: While about 95% of the genome was covered at 100X for 8 copies of virus, 98-99% of the genomes were covered at 100X for 22 to 675,885 copies of virus at an average sequencing depth of 5,000 reads per amplicon

questions.question: What sequencing-depth trade-off was observed when subsampling clinical libraries?

options.A: At 150,000 reads, at least 93% reached 100X; at 100,000 reads, 86%; and at 50,000 reads, at least 58%
options.B: At 50,000 reads, 93% reached 100X; at 150,000 reads, only 58%
options.C: Only 1 million reads per sample yielded any 100X coverage
options.D: All three depths yielded identical genome coverage above 99%

questions.rationale: The coverage falls with shallower sequencing but remains substantial at tens to hundreds of thousands of total reads.
questions.evidence_quote: At least 93% of the genome was covered at 100X with 150,000 total reads, and 86% of the genome was covered at 100X with 100,000 total reads. Even at 50,000 total reads per library, at least 58% of the genome was covered at 100X

questions.question: How did the authors reduce the risk of reporting false SARS-CoV-2 mutations in the clinical genomes?

options.A: They required agreement of two independent algorithms and treated only variants above 60% allele frequency as empirically true
options.B: They called all variants above 1% frequency using one algorithm
options.C: They accepted mutations only if present in every specimen
options.D: They used electrophoresis peak sizes to call all nucleotide substitutions

questions.rationale: Cross-algorithm agreement and a high allele-frequency threshold were used for high-confidence mutation reporting.
questions.evidence_quote: The mutations in the SARS-CoV-2 genome from the 13 specimens were detected by two independently developed algorithms. Only those mutations that were detected by both methods were reported. Assuming all viral particles from a single patient contained identical mutations, mutations with frequencies (%AF) > 60% were considered to be empirically true.

questions.question: What caveat did the authors attach to low-frequency intra-host mutation calls?

options.A: Without UMIs, low viral input and shallow reads can create PCR/sequencing noise and false calls; variants below 20% may also be missed
options.B: Every variant below 60% is guaranteed to be true intra-host diversity
options.C: Low-frequency calls are unaffected by viral copy number or read depth
options.D: The 20% threshold was selected because it captures all mutations exactly

questions.rationale: The authors warn that low input and read depth can depress allele frequency and introduce noise, while the ≥20% cutoff sacrifices some true rare variants.
questions.evidence_quote: Some true intra-host mutations with %AF < 20% might be missed. Since no UMI was used in the multiplex PCR amplification, intra-host mutations might still be contaminated with noise originating from PCR amplification, even though a 20% cutoff was applied. The occurrence of such noise may be exacerbated by low viral copy inputs in the multiplex PCR, or low read depth per amplicon in sequencing.

questions.question: What feature made the metagenomic multiplex method more practical than untargeted metagenomic sequencing in the human-DNA background?

options.A: Random hexamer-adapters plus background removal yielded 80% SARS-CoV-2 and 78% mitochondrial target coverage using about 0.6 million reads
options.B: It depleted all human DNA chemically and required more than 100 million reads
options.C: It sequenced only SARS-CoV-2-specific amplicons and could not detect unknown pathogens
options.D: It achieved 13% viral read recovery only after host depletion

questions.rationale: The method enriched viral and mitochondrial regions without additional host depletion, requiring moderate sequencing depth.
questions.evidence_quote: In fact, our results showed that 16% of the recovered bases, or 13% of the recovered reads, were within the viral N and S genes (Fig. 4A and Supplemental Table 4 ). 80% of SARS-CoV-2 and 78% of mitochondrial targets were covered (Fig. 4B ), and their base coverage was significantly higher than for human targets (Fig. 4C ). In contrast, only 0.08% of human chromosomal regions were amplified.
